study.technique_notes: Six levels of one acquisition, confirmed by the user. No burned-in annotation, callipers, scale bar, or HU ROI on any frame, so nothing here is quantitatively anchored. Bulky soft tissue at both lateral field margins is consistent with shoulder girdle / proximal arms within the scan field.

frames.slice_level: Upper thorax, at or just above the aortic arch (approximately T2-T4). Trachea round and midline; no arch contour resolved.
frames.notes: First frame supplied. Pixels not attached — arrived as a conversation attachment rather than a file.

frames.slice_level: Carina / proximal main bronchi, approximately T5-T6. Airway seen centrally as a transverse lucency at the bifurcation.
frames.notes: Second frame supplied, caudal to the first. Hilar vascular branching well seen bilaterally at this level. Pixels not attached.

frames.slice_level: Below the carina, at the main bronchi / bronchus intermedius, approximately T6-T7. Both bronchi visible as paired lucencies within the mediastinum.
frames.notes: Third frame supplied, caudal to the carinal frame. Largest lung cross-section of the three, with pulmonary vessels radiating prominently from both hila as expected at this level. Broad homogeneous central mediastinal soft tissue corresponds to heart and great vessels, undifferentiated because the study is unenhanced. Pixels not attached.

frames.slice_level: Lower thorax at heart level, approximately T7-T8. Heart occupies most of the mediastinum; bronchus intermedius and left lower lobe bronchus visible as paired lucencies.
frames.notes: Fourth frame supplied, caudal to the main-bronchi frame. First frame in this study on which the lower lobes are substantially in view. Pixels not attached.

frames.slice_level: Lower thorax approaching the lung bases, approximately T8-T9. Heart occupies the central mediastinum; both lower lobes broadly in view.
frames.notes: Fifth frame supplied, caudal to the heart-level frame. This frame resolves the question left open on frame 4: the right lower lobe abnormality is extensive and structural, not crowded vasculature. Pixels not attached.

frames.slice_level: Lung bases approaching the diaphragm, approximately T9-T10. Lung cross-sections reducing; central soft tissue is heart with diaphragm and upper abdominal contents beginning to enter the field.
frames.notes: Sixth frame supplied, the most caudal so far. Shows the basal process to be bilateral rather than confined to the right, with a posterior and dependent predominance on both sides. Pixels not attached.

findings.location: right lower lobe, extending from the perihilar region laterally and posteriorly
findings.description: Extensive heterogeneous abnormality of the right lower lobe: irregular soft-tissue-density opacity intermixed with multiple small rounded and tubular air-density lucencies, on a background of coarse irregular reticular and branching lines, extending from the perihilar region laterally and posteriorly. The internal lucencies are the discriminating feature — normal vasculature does not contain air-density spaces within it. Most extensive on the two most caudal frames, with posterior and dependent predominance. On frame 4, one level cranial to where it first became convincing, the same process was visible only as a nodular and branching cluster posteromedially and was recorded at 'possible' certainty as probable crowded vasculature; that read has been superseded.

findings.location: left lower lobe, posterior and dependent
findings.description: Clustered small nodular and short branching opacities with intervening lucencies in the posterior and dependent left lower lobe, similar in character to the right-sided process but less extensive, with the anterior left lung remaining well aerated. Not clearly abnormal one level cranial, where the left lower lobe territory was described as comparatively spared — whether that reflects a more caudal distribution on the left or an under-call on the frame above cannot be settled from these frames.

impression: Six contiguous axial levels of an unenhanced chest CT on soft-tissue window, descending from the upper thorax to the lung bases. The upper three levels are unremarkable. The lower three demonstrate a bilateral basal parenchymal process, right greater than left, with posterior and dependent predominance. On the right there is extensive heterogeneous opacity containing multiple small rounded and tubular air-density lucencies on a background of coarse reticular and branching lines. On the left, evident on the most caudal frame, there are clustered small nodular and short branching opacities of similar character but lesser extent, with the anterior left lung well aerated. The left-sided involvement was not apparent one level cranial, so the process is either more caudal on the left or was under-called there; these frames cannot distinguish those. The abnormality is definitely present and is not vascular — vessels do not contain air-density lucencies. Its nature is not settled here: bronchiectasis with mucus plugging, aspiration or bronchopneumonia, and chronic infection with bronchiolitis are all live considerations, with fibrotic change less likely given the asymmetry. No pneumothorax and no large pleural collection at the levels imaged; airway patent and midline throughout; bones intact. This is a significant bilateral finding that warrants review of the actual study on a lung window, with clinical context, rather than any conclusion drawn from screenshots.

differential.entity: Bronchiectasis with mucus plugging, with or without chronic infection
supporting: Tubular and rounded air-density lucencies within opacity, consistent with dilated airways
Bilateral lower lobe predominance is the classic distribution
Clustered nodular components fit mucus-filled small airways
against: Airway calibre relative to the accompanying artery cannot be judged on this window

supporting: Posterior and dependent distribution on both sides
Right greater than left, matching the more vertical right bronchial anatomy
Patchy clustered opacity with air bronchograms rather than a lobar pattern
against: No clinical context, symptom duration, or history supplied
The reticular background looks more established than a purely acute process

differential.entity: Chronic infection with tree-in-bud bronchiolitis, including mycobacterial disease
supporting: Clustered small nodular and branching opacities
against: Tree-in-bud cannot be confirmed on a soft-tissue window — it is a lung-window diagnosis

differential.entity: Fibrosis with traction bronchiectasis or honeycombing
against: The lucencies look more like airways than stacked honeycomb cysts
Marked right-left asymmetry is against a symmetric fibrotic process

differential.entity: Dependent atelectasis or partial volume with the diaphragm
supporting: Basal frames are prone to partial volume averaging
against: Neither explains the internal air-density lucencies, the nodular clustering, or the extent seen three levels cranial

limitations: Six axial levels only. The costophrenic angles and upper abdomen still were not reached, so the inferior extent of the basal process remains unknown and may continue below the lowest frame supplied.

Soft-tissue window on all five frames. This is the central limitation for the finding that matters: distinguishing bronchiectasis from consolidation from honeycombing requires a lung window, and none of these frames can do it. Airway-to-artery calibre, the basis of a bronchiectasis call, is not judgeable here.

Both lower lobe findings are recorded as present but uncharacterised. The differential is genuinely open and its ordering is not a conclusion. The left-sided finding is at 'probable' certainty because it is less extensive and closer to what dependent change can mimic.

Basal frames are the most vulnerable to partial volume averaging with the diaphragm, which raises apparent density at the lung bases. This does not explain the internal lucencies or the nodular clustering, but it does mean the apparent extent at the most caudal level may be overstated.
Non-contrast. Mediastinal and hilar nodes cannot be distinguished from unopacified vessels, so nodal assessment accompanying this lung abnormality is impossible.

No clinical context supplied — no age, sex, symptoms, duration, or history. Acute infection and chronic airway disease look far more alike on one unenhanced frame than they do with a history attached.
No DICOM metadata. Contrast phase, window, and slice levels are inferred from appearance; slice thickness and study date are unknown.
No burned-in callipers, scale bar, or HU ROI, so the extent of the abnormality is described but not measured.
Single acquisition, confirmed by the user. No prior and no follow-up in the base, so nothing establishes whether this is acute, chronic, or changing.
notes: First case in the base. Upper three levels are a normal-appearing thoracic reference; the lower three carry a significant bilateral basal abnormality, right greater than left. Finding was initially logged on frame 4 as 'rll-posteromedial-opacity' at possible certainty and attributed to crowded vasculature; frame 5 superseded that and the finding was renamed to 'rll-heterogeneous-opacity' and upgraded to definite. No comparison had been run against the old slug, so no comparison history was broken by the rename. Image pixels not attached for any frame — all six screenshots arrived as conversation attachments rather than files.
